title_original: Rafael Pavarotti: “Image-making is an act of restitution”
excerpt_original: Brazilian artist has put color and Black bodies at the center of fashion photography. The Musée des Arts Décoratifs is giving him his first exhibition in France, on view through May 2, 2027. L’article Rafael Pavarotti: “Image-making is an act of restitution” est apparu en…

blocks.text: Born in Belém, deep in the Amazon, Rafael Pavarotti passed through Rio, São Paulo, and London before setting down his bags in Paris and establishing himself, in barely a decade, as one of the most singular photographic voices of his generation. In the studio, he works against vivid backdrops that have become his signature: red, pink, purple, green, the colors of his Amazonian childhood. His models, most of them Black, from Africa or its diasporas, pose in majesty, frontal and sculptural. The Musée des Arts Décoratifs brings together more than 130 prints, from covers for the world’s leading fashion magazines to portraits of Rihanna, Harry Styles, and Beyoncé. Sébastien Quéquet, curator of the exhibition and head of the museum’s photographic collections in Paris, spoke with the photographer at length. Interview.
Sébastien Quéquet: Can you tell me about your childhood and the way in which your family shaped your personality and your approach to art?

Rafael Pavarotti: I was born in the heart of the Amazon, in Icoaraci, a district of Belém do Pará, in northern Brazil. Being born there was a foundational force. The Amazon is vast, saturated, dense with humidity and light. Color reigns there in expansion. Vegetation grows with urgency. The atmosphere is laden with intensity in every direction. That magnitude formed my earliest way of seeing. It shaped my relationship to scale, to presence, to excess as a natural rather than an extraordinary thing.

I grew up in a family of artisans. Craftsmanship was woven into daily life, present in the rhythm of work, in the patience required to complete an object properly, in the respect given to materials. My father, an artist, built our family business producing handmade leather bags and later custom furniture. Every seam, every cut, every joint carried intention. Through him I learned that quality issues from attention, and that manual work demands discipline, devotion, and responsibility. This importance of know-how was the basis of my ethics before it shaped my aesthetics.

I became aware of the importance of color through both the place it holds in landscapes and in domestic spaces. In Belém, color operates with instinct and conviction. Houses are painted in bold combinations. Clothing is assembled through intuition. There is confidence in chromatic expression, a comfort with saturation and contrast. My grandmother remains one of my deepest influences. Red is her favorite color, and her home carries a chromatic language of its own. As a child, I observed her carefully. She taught me that daring in the use of color is not about provocation, it is about sincerity. From her, I inherited a sense of courage in composition and an understanding that color carries emotional authority.

blocks.caption: “Peacocks on the Move,” W Magazine , September 2025. © Rafael Pavarotti

blocks.text: In what way has this relation to the Amazon and nature influenced your work until now?

I was born within one of the most powerful ecological and spiritual territories on Earth. I grew up surrounded by rivers, by igarapés that run through the forest like veins. I learned to swim when I was very young, and water became my first language. I was always immersed in it. The forest was not a place you crossed fortuitously, but a permanent presence. I built tree houses, I spent entire days moving through that environment, teaching myself through proximity rather than through formal education. Everything I understood about the world came through direct experience with nature.

The Amazon teaches a different relationship to time. In the heart of the forest, time loses its authority. There are no clear markers of a century or a period there. The rhythm is governed by cycles that extend beyond industrial or colonial structures of measurement. That experience taught me to observe, to listen, to know that existence unfolds through attention rather than control.

There is also a spiritual dimension that shaped my comprehension of the forest. I grew up in proximity to ancestral knowledge, to forms of healing and cosmologies that considered nature as a living intelligence rather than a passive resource. Entering the forest always inspired me with deep respect. It required awareness, humility, and permission. This link allowed me to envisage nature not as scenery, but as an organism that sustains life at every level.

As I grew older, I began to comprehend the political reality surrounding the Amazon, this territory under constant pressure, historically modeled by extraction, exploitation, and erasure. I became aware that its preservation is inseparable from the survival of the planet itself. That awareness increased my feeling of responsibility, not only toward the land, but toward representation and cultural memory.
How did you train yourself in photography?

Photography entered my life through proximity, long before I understood it as a profession or even as a medium. My father used to photograph our family when I was a child. I remember watching him closely, with a kind of silent admiration. He was my first reference, my first example of presence and care. He was the person who shaped my earliest reading of the world. Seeing him hold a camera carried meaning beyond the act itself, connected to memory, to the desire to preserve something that mattered.

There was also a photographer in our community. He was the only photographer in the area, and his presence carried a certain aura. Everyone went to him to be photographed. I spent a lot of time around him, observing how people positioned themselves in front of his camera, the quiet transformation that happened when someone became the subject of an image. Even then, I grasped that photography had the power to affirm existence.

When I was 12 years old, I found my father’s camera and took it to school without telling him. I asked my friends if I could photograph them. That moment marked the beginning of a practice that felt immediately natural to me.

My curiosity was never directed toward landscape or objects. It was always toward people. I was drawn to presence, to the complexity that could be read in someone’s face, in their posture, in their silence. Photography became a means of entering that space of encounter. Photography, for me, has always been rooted in the act of seeing another person fully. Every portrait is an exchange. It requires trust, attention, and openness. Through that process, I not only discover the person in front of the camera, I also discover something about myself. That relationship remains at the core of my practice today.

blocks.caption: “Floral Study,” Perfect Magazine , September 2023. © Rafael Pavarotti

blocks.text: Can you talk about your departure for Rio de Janeiro. Was it for fashion?

One of the most decisive moments happened when I was 12 years old, when I was still living with my parents. A friend showed me the video of a Christian Dior show directed by John Galliano. It was the Haute Couture Spring-Summer 2004 collection, inspired by ancient Egypt, accompanied by the sound of “Baby Boy” by Beyoncé. I remember watching it in complete stillness. Something shifted in my perception. I understood, watching this video, that I now wanted to work in that sector.

My departure for Rio de Janeiro when I was 15 was not a rupture, but a continuation of something that had already begun as I had participated in organizing Fashion Week in Belém. I wanted to expand my possibilities and to position my work within a larger cultural and professional ecosystem. Fashion had been present in my life from the very beginning, long before I understood it as an industry or a profession. It existed as a cultural language, as a form of expression embedded in the environment where I was raised. Where I come from, fashion has always been a form of social and cultural articulation. I grew up surrounded by the visual power of celebrations such as the Boi Bumbá, the Festas Juninas, the Círio de Nazaré, and the sound systems of tecnobrega and carimbó. All of them were occasions during which clothing carried meaning, where adornment expressed identity, ancestry and belonging. Fashion was never distant from life. It was a living language.
How did the commissions from Vogue arrive so quickly?

I arrived in Rio to work on Fashion Week at 15 and then for two years, I immersed myself in the local fashion environment. I met models and photographed some of them to create their books. I also spent time in agencies, and dedicated all of my free time to photographing. I was working as a waiter then, and every day away from the restaurant became an opportunity to create. I did not yet own a camera. I relied on the generosity of friends, borrowing equipment and learning through continuous practice.

Two years after my arrival, at the age of 17, I received an email from the creative director of Vogue Brasil, who had seen one of my books and asked if I would be available for a shoot a few days later. It was the beginning of my collaboration with Vogue . Entering that environment at a young age brought both excitement and responsibility. It was my first experience working within a structure of that scale, surrounded by people whose lives were fully dedicated to image-making. I approached in an open attitude, aware that I was stepping into a space shaped by a long visual tradition.

blocks.caption: Rihanna, Perfect Magazine , June 2024. © Rafael Pavarotti
“The Line of Time,” Vogue , May 2023. © Rafael Pavarotti

blocks.text: In the history of fashion photography, as in fashion in general, racialized people have been underrepresented, and when they have been, it has often been as a fleeting phenomenon or for tokenism. Is this situation a starting point for your work?

The fashion industry, like many cultural systems, was built upon historical exclusions that still continue to structure it today. While there have been visible shifts in recent years, representation cannot function as an isolated gesture. There must be a sustained commitment to it. In 2020, I photographed the first campaign in the history of Dior composed entirely of Black models. In 2023, I photographed the first campaign in Balmain’s history for which only Black women posed. These moments carried weight because they disrupted longstanding patterns of absence. At the same time, they revealed the structural distance that the fashion institutions still had to cross.

In February 2022, I photographed a cover with Edward Enninful for British Vogue titled “As the World Turns.” It was the first time that this magazine’s cover was constructed around the presence of nine dark-skinned women simultaneously. That image constituted a structural rupture within the visual language of fashion media. It was not simply a cover, but a shift in what until then had been considered permissible in this media space. The reactions revealed the depth of that rupture. The cover was met with significant criticism, exposing the resistance that manifested itself when long-established visual hierarchies are confronted and destabilized. That reaction made perceptible the underlying tensions that continue to shape the industry. It also validated the necessity of the work. It became clear to me that such images do more than represent individuals, they alter perception and open space so that new visual realities can exist.

My response has been driven by clarity. I conceive my presence within this field as part of a broader movement shaped by those who came before me, thinkers, artists, and leaders who articulated the importance of autonomy, self-definition, and intellectual sovereignty. Their work established the conditions for new generations to exist unapologetically. What protects the work from being reduced to symbolism is the authorship. It’s what describes intention. It defines the way in which the image is thought, how the subject is encountered, and how meaning is produced. When the authorship remains intact, the image cannot be separated from the consciousness that shaped it. The work itself becomes the answer, a continuous confirmation of existence, of thought, and of autonomy. It does not depend on validation to remain meaningful. It is because it must be.
How can the fashion industry move toward more open, inclusive, and ethical practices?

Change does not emerge from singular events. It is built through continuity, through repetition, which facilitate structural integration. The responsibility does not belong to one image, one campaign, or one individual. It belongs to the industry as a whole. From the beginning, my intention was not simply to produce images in the framework of an existing structure, but to participate in its transformation. My work has always been grounded in the people and communities that shaped my comprehension of the world, particularly Black and Indigenous communities. That foundation remains central to my practice. At the same time, I understand diversity as an in-situ condition that extends beyond fixed categories. It reflects the multiplicity inherent in human existence. Living and working across different geographies has reinforced this awareness. It has confirmed the necessity of resisting visual monocultures and embracing plurality as a fundamental principle.

Representation, when detached from responsibility, can easily become symbolic rather than structural. It can be used to create the appearance of transformation without changing the conditions that made exclusion possible in the first place. I am quite aware that visibility alone does not guarantee change. Image has the capacity to validate, but it can also be used to neutralize, to absorb difference without allowing it to alter the underlying structure. This tension has always existed within cultural production.
Among those who came before you, who are the most inspiring?

Tribute, in my work, is a form of recognition. It is a way of acknowledging those whose life, thought, and courage have expanded the possibilities of those who came after them. These figures carry forms of knowledge that extend beyond their own lives. They model how we conceive dignity, resistance, and imagination.

Maya Angelou is one of those presences. Her voice carried clarity, strength, and an unwavering commitment to truth. She understood language as a tool capable of restoring what had been denied or silenced. Her work validated the importance of existing fully.

Carolina Maria de Jesus also played a fundamental role. Her writing resulted from lived experience, from conditions that attempted to erase her visibility, and yet she transformed that reality into testimony. Her words carry precision and urgency. They remind us that the authorship does not depend on permission. It is born from necessity.

There are also ancestral figures whose presence transcends historical record. Dandara and Zumbi dos Palmares embody forms of resistance rooted in autonomy and collective survival. Their destiny continues to resonate so that the freedom that has always been built through courage and continuity is not forgotten.

Contemporary thinkers and leaders such as Ailton Krenak, Raoni Metuktire, and Geni Núñez have also oriented my conception of existence, responsibility, and collective balance. Their words invite a reconsideration of how we relate to the world and to one another, and they offer pathways toward ways of living grounded in awareness and continuity.

People other than public figures have influenced me. My family shaped my earliest conceptions of resilience, care, and imagination. My friends, my community, the people who have walked beside me, remain among my greatest sources of inspiration. They exist outside institutional recognition, yet their impact is immeasurable.

blocks.caption: “Extreme Beauty,” Vogue Italia, September 2019. © Rafael Pavarotti

blocks.text: Your work often brings up the themes of time, history, but also the future that has to be written. What message do you want to convey through the concepts of heritage, roots, and future generations?

My work comes out of an awareness that we exist within a continuum. We are shaped by those who came before us, and at the same time, we carry a responsibility toward those who will come after. Image, for me, operates within that space. It allows memory, presence, and possibility to coexist.

I come from a lineage where much of our history, knowledge, and memory was never formally archived as an important document. Knowledge was transmitted through gesture, through oral histories, through ways of living that were not always recognized in official records. Photography became a means of taking part in that continuity, to create images that validate existence and preserve forms of presence that might otherwise remain invisible.

Heritage, in my understanding, is not static. It is something that continues to unfold. It exists in the body, in posture, in expression, in how someone occupies space. My work pays attention to these different aspects. It seeks to create images that carry dignity and permanence, images thanks to which people see themselves not as fragments, but as part of a larger historical and cultural trajectory.

At the same time, my work is deeply connected to what has not yet been written. I am interested in contributing to a visual future in which more inclusive forms of representation circulate, where younger generations encounter images that expand their sense of what is possible, where future generations can get their bearings with clarity, strength, and belonging. The act of creating these images is connected to the belief that visibility has the power to shape consciousness.

blocks.caption: “Sheila Bawar,” Perfect Magazine , August 2025. © Rafael Pavarotti

blocks.text: How do you think the role of image-making shapes historical consciousness?

Human beings have always used images to know themselves. Long before written language emerged, images were already serving as vessels of memory, transmitting knowledge, belief, and identity across time. From the cave paintings of Tassili n’Ajjer in Africa, to the visual systems of ancient Egypt, to the material cultures of Indigenous peoples in the Amazon, images existed as a way to preserve experience and to give form to existence itself.

In many African civilizations, image was not separate from life. Sculptures, masks, and symbols were understood as extensions, carrying spiritual, social, and historical meaning. These visual forms allowed knowledge to move across generations, ensuring continuity beyond the limits of a single lifetime.

Similarly, in Indigenous cultures of the Amazon, images have always functioned as a living archive, embedded in the body, in objects, and in the environment. Through body painting, material construction, and ritual, images become vectors of a memory and help transmit ancestral knowledge. Images do not simply record what exists. They participate in materializing what becomes perceptible, and what becomes remembered. Historical consciousness is formed not only through events, but through what remains visible over time. What is seen repeatedly becomes part of collective understanding. What is absent risks being forgotten. Because of this, image-making carries profound responsibility. I understand my work as part of an ongoing expansion of this visual field. Creating images offers me the possibility of contributing to the construction of memory in a way that reflects a broader and more truthful spectrum of human existence. Each image is a snapshot of the present, but it also moves forward, becoming part of the visual foundation through which future generations will understand this time.
What responsibilities come with authorship when working in the framework of systems that historically excluded certain bodies and identities?

The authorship in these systems requires being aware of these exclusions. It necessitates understanding that the creation of images has never existed outside of power, and that visibility has always been shaped by structures that determined who could be seen, and who could create.

For a long time, many lives existed outside the visual archives or appeared only through narratives drawn up by others. This absence was not passive. It influenced how humanity came to portray itself, and whose lives were recognized as central or peripheral. This produced fractures of the visual field, shaping what was allowed to exist visibly and what remained outside of recognition. Entire populations were excluded from the visual archives. This absence shaped how humanity came to see itself.

To create images today is to enter into a direct relationship with that history. It means recognizing that every photograph contributes to the visual field that determines collective memory. Because of this, the authorship needs clarity. It demands having the courage to create without reproducing inherited shackles, and to allow new forms of visibility to emerge with autonomy and dignity. For me, image-making is inseparable from the act of reclaiming space, memory, and narrative. To create an image is to take part in the restoration of visual sovereignty.

In this sense, image-making is an act of restitution. It restores continuity between existence and representation, allowing both to stand side by side, without fracture. Each image contributes to the visual archive that future generations will have a share in. To create is to participate in shaping how humanity will see itself, and how this moment will remain in history.

“As the World Turns” was an important moment in your career, in terms of visibility but also of reception. This series received a lot of comments for your plastic and photographic treatment of Black skins. What creates its specificity, what ideas do you call up?

The publication of an image is always a special moment. People look at it through the lens of their personal experience, which is never neutral, especially when you tackle the questions of Black skins, visibility, and representation. Certain people see the assertion of a power in this series, while others perceive an effacement in it, or, in front of it, feel a discomfort. It is a question here of the weight of history that the images convey. For me, the skin does not have a set and technical value. I focus on the ambience, the density, the presence, because I am trying to find the intensity, the light, and the temperature specific to Amazonia. Darkness is not simply dark. It carries a vibration, a depth, and a saturation that are part of my language. Darkness and blackness are not absence: they are the ancestral, the original, the silence, the intimacy, the transcendent. So when I work with color, shade, and skin, I don’t think in terms of correction or naturalism. I look for what dark skin transmits both of softness, of mystery, of spirituality, and of monumentality. It is completely the opposite of effacement.

blocks.caption: “The Surreal Deal,” W Magazine , June 2024. © Rafael Pavarotti

blocks.text: Can you talk about your freedom while you are working on a commission? Has it evolved now that you are more established?

Freedom has always been essential to how I work. From the very beginning, photography was not something I approached as a service, but as a way of articulating how I see and conceive the world. That relation has remained unchanged, regardless of scale or context.

As I began working within the fashion industry, I encountered structures that operate with their own histories, expectations, and frameworks. Entering those spaces required awareness, without however meaning that it surrenders to it. What I learned early on was the importance of coherence. I chose to work with people who recognized my perspective and trusted what I contribute. That trust became the foundation of a meaningful collaboration.

Fashion, at its best, is a collective process. It brings together different forms of the authorship. Taking part in that dynamic, my role has always been to maintain the clarity of my vision while remaining open to exchange. Collaboration enriches the work. It contributes new dimensions, new conversations, new possibilities. My creative process was never solitary. It was shaped through long-standing creative relationships built on trust, dialogue, and a shared vision. My collaboration with my close friend and creative partner IB Kamara is part of that continuum. Our work results from a shared commitment to expanding the field of representation and redefining the visual language of fashion. Together, we have created images that exist beyond the moment of their production, images that mark the history of photography as it continues to evolve, shaping its future… Collaboration does not diminish authorship when it is built on mutual respect.

There are always moments of resistance when working within any established system, whatever it is, and they are inherent in the nature of cultural production. Those moments never altered my sense of direction. They on the contrary increased my understanding of what must remain intact. Freedom, for me, is not granted by external structures. It exists as an internal condition. It is something I carry into every project, every encounter, every image.

blocks.caption: Rihanna, Perfect Magazine , June 2024. © Rafael Pavarotti
“The Line of Time,” Vogue , May 2023. © Rafael Pavarotti

blocks.text: What must photography protect today, why does the image continue to matter?

The image continues to matter because it is through it that we recognize ourselves. Not only physically, but psychologically. It allows us to know that we exist, to observe ourselves as part of the world. This has always been true, regardless of technology.

What has changed is that the image is no longer an isolated moment. It has become a condition of daily life. People live in front of cameras. They observe themselves, edit themselves, anticipate themselves. Appearance is constantly being constructed. For a time, this produced an intense pursuit of control and perfection. But perfection, when it becomes permanent, loses its force. It stops creating sensation. Everything begins to look the same. And when everything looks the same, the image is therefore no longer memorable.

Photography must protect the freedom to see without instruction. We live in a time in which images are constantly telling you how to feel, how to react, how you should interpret what you are looking at. Most images arrive already closed. There is no space left inside them.

What is important to me is to create images that remain open. Images that do not exhaust themselves in the first second. Images that continue to exist after you look at them, that linger somewhere in your mind without resolving completely. Otherwise, the image disappears at the exact moment it appears.
“Rafael Pavarotti. Photographer” is on view at the Musée des Arts Décoratifs (MAD) in Paris, through May 2, 2027.
The exhibition catalogue, Rafael Pavarotti, Photographer , is published by Musée des Arts Décoratifs Editions.
This interview first appeared in the exhibition catalogue Rafael Pavarotti, Photographer . We thank the Musée des Arts Décoratifs for allowing us to share it.
